1.pericope_label: And the Lord spake unto Moses, saying, See, I have called by name Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah: And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship, To devise cunning works, to work in gold, and in silver, and in brass, And in cutting of stones, to set them, and in carving of timber, to work in all manner of workmanship. And I, behold, I have given with him Aholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan: and in the hearts of all that are wise hearted I have put wisdom, that they may make all that I have commanded thee; The tabernacle of the congregation, and the ark of the testimony, and the mercy seat that is thereupon, and all the furniture of the tabernacle, And the table and his furniture, and the pure candlestick with all his furniture, and the altar of incense, And the altar of burnt offering with all his furniture, and the laver and his foot, And the cloths of service, and the holy garments for Aaron the priest, and the garments of his sons, to minister in the priest’s office, And the anointing oil, and sweet incense for the holy place: according to all that I have commanded thee shall they do.

schools.summary: Begin with the difficulty rather than the doctrine: the actual hardness of the work might have overwhelmed Moses and the whole people with despair, since this was no ordinary task on which the most skilful artificers might exercise their ingenuity but a marvellous structure whose pattern had been shown on the mount, and their servile employments in Egypt were such as would extinguish all intellectual vigour and prevent them aspiring to any liberal art. Draw from that the rule, that those who obediently follow God's voice are never destitute of his aid. Read the announcement of the workmen as forestalling exactly the doubt that would otherwise have risen in Moses' mind. On the calling by name, correct the Targums that paraphrase it as called with a good name: the idiom marks singular and personal choice to an office, not the imposing of a name — though the name is significant in any case, meaning in the shadow of God, so that a man so sheltered was fittingly set to make things which were themselves shadows of good things to come. Find it unsurprising that the principal workman should come from Judah, and account for a companion from Dan only by supposing that its obscurity the more highly illustrated the grace of God. Then face the apparent contradiction that God puts wisdom into those already wise-hearted: reject the common solution that special grace merely aids natural ability, and argue that whatever grows in us comes from the continued operation of the Spirit, the endowment already given being only the seed. Narrow the filling itself — not the special graces of the Spirit nor gifts for spiritual service, but ingenuity and skill in manual arts and mechanical operations.

Take the three nouns apart from their roots: wisdom as the compass of mind that judges what is best to be done, understanding as the capacity to distinguish the parts of a work and see how they connect, and knowledge as practical and experimental acquaintance with a person or thing. Collect pagan witnesses to the same instinct, quoting the Stoic that the seeds of all arts are implanted in us and God draws out the talent from concealment, and the Odyssey on the craftsman taught by Athene who overlays silver with gold. State the principle in a line: skill in common employments is the gift of God, who teaches the tradesman as well as the husbandman and must have the praise of it. Gloss the workman's name as under the especial protection of the Most High, and trace his descent through Hur to Judah by way of Pharez, Hezron and Caleb. On the furniture, distinguish the vestments for the ordinary work of the ministry from the garments peculiar to the high priest, and explain the pure candlestick either from the gold of which it was made, or the splendour of its workmanship, or the purest oil that was always burnt in it.

Say that it is a high honour to be called of God by name, since he so calls only those he appoints to some great work — Moses, Samuel, Cyrus. Report that the grandfather is generally supposed identical with the Hur who supported Moses's hands and was left joint regent with Aaron, while cautioning that there is no evidence for this beyond the identity of the name. Distinguish the two workmen's spheres: the first man's work was general, the second's special, and though our version styles him engraver, cunning workman and embroiderer, nothing is said of engraving in the original, the true meaning being that he had charge of the textile fabrics and directed both the weaving and the embroidery without intermeddling in other matters. Note that the tribe of Dan is among the most undistinguished and yet produced two great artists, this man and the master workman employed on Solomon's temple. On the cloths of service, set the modern critics who take them for the state robes of the high priest against the rabbinical interpreters who understand the cloths in which the ark and other vessels were wrapped when the camp moved — then propose that both the garments of Aaron and those of his sons are included, the later clauses being exegetical of the first.

State the practical problem first: a great deal of fine work had been ordered and the people were to provide the materials, but who should put them into form? Moses was learned in all the learning of the Egyptians and acquainted with the visions of the Almighty, yet he knew not how to engrave or embroider; and the Israelites, having lived all their days in bondage, knew how to make brick and work in clay but had never been brought up to work in gold or cut diamonds, so that goldsmiths and jewellers would have to be made out of masons and bricklayers. Suppose there were enough who would gladly be employed and would do their best, but that it would be hard to find a proper person to preside over the work — and then let the answer come from God's naming of one.

debates.question: What does being called by name signify?

sides.position: A high honour reserved for those appointed to some great work, as Moses, Samuel and Cyrus were
Singular and personal choice to an office, not the imposing of a name — against the Targums that render it called with a good name
Particular appointment to be chief superintendent of the whole work

debates.question: If they were already wise-hearted, what did the new gift add?

sides.position: Nothing is added to nature: whatever grows in us comes from the continued operation of the Spirit, the earlier endowment being only the seed
Those with a natural genius received an increase of wisdom by immediate inspiration, so that they knew how to execute the work
Not the special graces of the Spirit nor gifts for spiritual service, but ingenuity and skill in manual arts
Skill in common employments is simply the gift of God, who puts even this wisdom into the inward parts

debates.question: What are the cloths of service?

sides.position: The state robes of the high priest, on the judgement of the modern critics
The cloths in which the ark and the other vessels were wrapped when the camp moved, on the rabbinical interpretation
Vestments for the ordinary work of the ministry, distinguished from the garments peculiar to the high priest

outliers.note: Alone reaches outside Scripture for corroboration, quoting the Stoic that the seeds of all arts are implanted in us and drawn out by God, and the Odyssey on the craftsman taught by Athene, to show that even the heathen acknowledged that talents come from God.

Alone treats the wisdom given to the already wise-hearted as a theological problem, rejects the received solution that grace merely assists natural ability, and makes the earlier endowment no more than a seed requiring the Spirit’s continued operation.

themes: I have called by name Bezaleel
filled him with the spirit of God
in the hearts of all that are wise hearted

12.pericope_label: And the Lord spake unto Moses, saying, Speak thou also unto the children of Israel, saying, Verily my sabbaths ye shall keep: for it is a sign between me and you throughout your generations; that ye may know that I am the Lord that doth sanctify you. Ye shall keep the sabbath therefore; for it is holy unto you: every one that defileth it shall surely be put to death: for whosoever doeth any work therein, that soul shall be cut off from among his people. Six days may work be done; but in the seventh is the sabbath of rest, holy to the Lord: whosoever doeth any work in the sabbath day, he shall surely be put to death. Wherefore the children of Israel shall keep the sabbath, to observe the sabbath throughout their generations, for a perpetual covenant. It is a sign between me and the children of Israel for ever: for in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he rested, and was refreshed.

schools.summary: Explain why the command is repeated here: it is quite in its proper place, inasmuch as the thought might easily have occurred that it was allowable to omit the keeping of the sabbath while such a work was in hand, and the repetition comes with the threat of death and extermination renewed in the most solemn manner. On the sign, make it a replacement: circumcision had been given as the covenant sign to Abraham and his descendants, but its adoption by many heathen nations had left it no longer a distinguishing mark by which God's people could certainly be known, so a new sign was needed; the observance of one day in seven proved effectual because it was not likely to be adopted by the heathen and in fact was not, and it was still regarded as the special badge of a Jew in the latest period of the nation, as the Roman satirists attest. Call the death penalty a new enactment and tie it to the new dignity the day had acquired, since the sabbath-breaker now threw himself out of covenant with God and did what in him lay to throw the whole people out, so that the penalty is in no way surprising but accords with the general spirit of the code; gloss cutting off as separation, excommunication in fact. Then set the ground of the whole observance in the creation, so that man is through it made like his Maker, having from time to time a rest from his labours as God had, and thereby realising the blessedness of that final rest which remains for the people of God.

Reason from the severity back to the institution: we gather the dignity and excellency of the mystery from God deeming an apparently light transgression of it worthy of death. Hold the offence to be no excusable contempt but a professed overthrow of the mark God had set as a distinction between his people and heathen nations, since by neglect of the day religion itself would be cast down and trampled. Note that the prohibition of kindling fire anticipates the glosses the people would have been ready enough to invent, and that the passages following would be superfluous repetition were the people not thus reminded that the matter was of the utmost importance. Then limit the perpetuity: the for ever is like the everlasting possession of the land, the covenant of circumcision, the passover and the fast of atonement, reaching to the end of the Jewish world and state at the coming of Christ, when a new state of things began.

Read the sign in two directions at once, as a great instance of God's favour in distinguishing them from all other people and as a great instance of their duty in observing it; God, by sanctifying the day among them, let them know that he sanctified them and set them apart for his service. Add the historical claim: by keeping one day in seven they testified that they worshipped the God who made the world in six days, and so distinguished themselves from nations who, having first lost the sabbath and with it the memorial of the creation, by degrees lost the knowledge of the Creator and gave the creature the honour due to him alone. Supply the procedure for the penalty, that the magistrates were to examine and the guilty be stoned, and explain the cutting off by the offender's infidelity. Then hold the observance still binding as type: because the day is a sign of the future rest and blessedness, its religious observance must be perpetually kept up, and the type must continue in force till the antitype come. Note that the day is holy unto you, designed for your benefit as well as for God's honour; and take the divine rest and refreshment as spoken in condescension to human weakness, since a man who religiously rests will find both body and soul refreshed.

Trace how often the law has already been given — before any other law by way of preparation, then in the body of the moral law as the fourth commandment, then annexed to the judicial law, and now added to the first part of the ceremonial — and give the reason for that pattern: the observance of the sabbath is the hem and hedge of the whole law, standing in the moral law between the two tables, so that where no conscience is made of it, farewell both godliness and honesty. Then supply the occasion here: orders had been given that a tabernacle be set up and furnished with all possible expedition, and lest they should think the nature of the work and the haste required would justify labouring at it on sabbath days to get it done the sooner, the caution is seasonably inserted — though they must hasten the work, they must not break the rest.

debates.question: Why is the sabbath law repeated at this point?

sides.position: Because the thought might easily have occurred that it was allowable to omit the sabbath while such a work was in hand
Because it is the hem and hedge of the whole law, and has therefore been attached to each part of the law in turn
Because repetition was needed to remind the people that the matter was of the utmost importance

debates.question: Why was a new covenant sign needed?

sides.position: Because circumcision had been adopted by many heathen nations and was no longer distinguishing, whereas the seventh day was not adopted by them and proved effectual
Because the day testified that they worshipped the God who made the world in six days, distinguishing them from nations that had lost the memorial of creation

debates.question: How long does the sign last?

sides.position: To the end of the Jewish world and state at the coming of Christ, as with the land, circumcision and the passover
The type must continue in force till the antitype come, so the observance must be perpetually kept up
It points past both to the final rest that remains for the people of God

outliers.note: Alone explains the sabbath sign as a replacement for a failed one, arguing that circumcision had ceased to distinguish God’s people once the heathen adopted it, and citing the Roman satirists to show the seventh day still served as the badge of a Jew centuries later.

Alone limits the perpetuity of the sign to the end of the Jewish state, setting the for ever of the sabbath beside that of the land, circumcision and the passover, against a reading that keeps the type in force until the antitype comes.

themes: verily my sabbaths ye shall keep
it is a sign between me and you

18.pericope_label: And he gave unto Moses, when he had made an end of communing with him upon mount Sinai, two tables of testimony, tables of stone, written with the finger of God.

schools.summary: Set the moment in its sequence: the voice had already been heard from the fire, the ten commandments delivered, the form of the tabernacle described and the work already finished by the artificers though not yet dedicated, and Moses was then withdrawn again from the sight and intercourse of men. Ask why forty days were needed at all, and answer that though the ten commandments comprised the sum of the doctrine and might suffice for the rule of a pious life, a clearer exposition was required, so that Moses was taken into the sanctuary of heaven to learn familiarly all that concerned their full understanding, since he could never have reached their genuine meaning had God not been his master and teacher. Draw two conclusions: that the five books were written not only under the guidance of the Spirit but as God himself suggested them, and that all true pastors ought likewise to be disciples, teaching nothing but what they have received — the forty days' silence being so that he might afterwards speak freely by the authority of God. Then give the division of the ten between the stones: five on each, or rather four on the first, that being the largest and containing the duty owed to God, and six on the second, which regard the duty of men to one another; and observe that the whole reduces to love to God and love to neighbour.

Argue that the writing was performed and not merely commanded, stringing four passages together: the promise of tables which God says he has written, this verse on the finger of God, the later statement that the tables were the work of God and the writing his writing graven upon them, and the summary that he added no more but wrote them on two tables of stone. Add the conjecture from a history of knowledge that this may have been the first writing in alphabetical characters ever exhibited to the world, though marks or hieroglyphics cut in wood and stone existed before; and explain the choice of material by the purpose, that the record might be lasting because the testimony was meant for future generations. Distinguish further, that the stone tables were not prepared by Moses but probably by the ministry of angels, while the writing was by God's will and power immediately, without the use of any instrument. Explain the name: they are called tables of testimony because the written law testified the will of God concerning them and would be a testimony against them if they disobeyed.

Make the closing verse the point the whole preceding design has been running towards, and argue it by nesting the containers: the court presupposed the tabernacle; the outer chamber was a mere vestibule to the inner; the inner chamber was a receptacle for the ark; and the ark was a chest constructed to contain the two tables. So the delivery is the termination and crown of the entire conference on the mountain, and putting that treasure into Moses' hands was a first step towards carrying out a design laid down with a view to it. Note that the definite article should stand, giving the two tables rather than two, since these are the ones glanced at earlier and distinctly promised before the ascent. Then decline to go beyond what the text allows: the tables were inscribed by some supernatural process and not by any human hand, but the exact nature of that process is not revealed to us.

sides.position: Inscribed by some supernatural process and not by any human hand, the exact nature of it not revealed to us
Written by the power and not merely the command of God, on the evidence of four passages taken together
The stone prepared probably by the ministry of angels, the writing by God's will and power immediately, without the use of any instrument

debates.question: How are the ten divided between the two stones?

sides.position: Five on each; or rather four on the first, that being the largest and containing the duty owed to God, and six on the second
Two tables because the law directs us in our duty towards God and towards man

debates.question: Why were forty days needed for what the ten commandments already contained?

sides.position: Because a clearer exposition was required, which Moses could never have reached had God not been his master and teacher
The delivery of the tables is the crown of the whole conference, the treasure with a view to which every direction about the sanctuary had been given

outliers.note: Alone raises the question of writing itself, reporting the conjecture that these tables may have carried the first alphabetic writing ever exhibited to the world, marks and hieroglyphics on wood and stone having preceded it.

Alone asks why forty days were needed for what the ten commandments already contained, and answers with a claim about the Pentateuch, that Moses wrote his five books as God himself suggested them, so that all true pastors must likewise teach nothing but what they have received.

themes: written with the finger of God
